opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: if you look at what models can do today on any individual step, they're already incredibly capable. Give a frontier model a well-scoped problem, a hard math question, a tricky function to write, a document to analyze, and it'll often do as well as a strong human expert, sometimes better. Raw intelligence on a single step is no longer the bottleneck.

What breaks down is stringing those steps together over hours, days, or weeks, in an open-ended environment, without someone hovering over it. Errors compound. If you're 99% reliable per step and the task takes a thousand steps, you basically never finish. Humans aren't perfect per step either, but we notice when we've gone off track, we recover, we re-plan, we remember what we were doing and why. That error-correction loop over a long horizon is what's still missing.

The "general-domain" part matters too. We've seen long-horizon reliability in narrow settings. In games like poker, or in coding where you have tests and compilers giving you a crisp signal, you can train for robustness because the environment tells you when you're wrong. In the messy real world, with ambiguous goals, sparse feedback, and situations nobody anticipated, you don't get that signal for free. The system has to build its own sense of "is this going well?" and act on it.

So I call it the last big problem because once you have an agent that can reliably pursue a goal over a long horizon in any domain, and can be trusted to recover from its own mistakes, you've essentially got something that can do most economically valuable work. Everything else, better reasoning, more knowledge, faster inference, either already works well or follows naturally from scaling. Reliability over time is the piece that turns a very smart assistant into something you can actually delegate to. That's the gap between a tool and a colleague.

r001.rationale: The response says single-step capabilities such as reasoning, knowledge, and coding already work well or improve with scaling, making long-horizon reliability the remaining gap.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning or argue that it would help achieve long-horizon reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I'd frame it is this: if you look at what's actually happened over the last few years, almost every capability that people once pointed to as "the hard part" has fallen. Reasoning on math problems, writing code, understanding images, following nuanced instructions, even things like humor and style. Within a single step, or a short sequence of steps, these models are often superhuman or close to it.

But there's a gap between being brilliant for five minutes and being dependable for five days. And that gap is where almost all the economic value sits. Most real work isn't a single clever answer. It's hundreds or thousands of small decisions chained together, where you have to notice when you've drifted, recover from mistakes, keep track of what you actually know versus what you assumed, and not confidently plow ahead when the ground has shifted under you. Humans are not perfect at this either, but we have a kind of self-correcting loop that lets a competent person run a project for months without the whole thing collapsing.

The reason I think it's the last big problem, rather than just one more on the list, is that it isn't a narrow skill you can patch with a bigger dataset. Reliability over long horizons is compositional. If you have a one percent chance of a serious unrecoverable error per step, then over a thousand steps you almost certainly fail. So you don't just need the model to be a bit better. You need it to be good at a fundamentally different thing: knowing when it's uncertain, checking its own work, asking the right question at the right time, and maintaining a coherent picture of the task as the context grows and shifts. Those are the properties that let errors stay local instead of cascading.

And "general-domain" is the other half that matters. It's not that hard to make a system reliable in one narrow environment where you can hand-craft the guardrails. The challenge is doing it across arbitrary tasks, in messy real settings you didn't anticipate, where the agent has to figure out the structure of the problem on its own. That's what separates a tool from something that actually behaves like a colleague you can delegate to.

So my view is that once you crack that, there isn't much left that looks like a fundamental research barrier. Everything else becomes engineering, scaling, and distribution. That's why I think of it as the last big one, and it's also why it's the thing I spend most of my time thinking about.

r001.rationale: It says many other major capabilities have advanced or been solved, then frames long-horizon reliability as the remaining major problem.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning or argue that it would help achieve reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because there’s a big difference between being able to do each individual step of a task and being able to reliably finish the whole thing. A model can give you a really impressive answer, write a useful piece of code, or solve a hard problem, and still struggle when it has to make hundreds of decisions in sequence.

Over a long horizon, small mistakes accumulate. You misunderstand something early on, build on that misunderstanding, and end up somewhere completely wrong. And the challenge isn’t just avoiding mistakes. It’s noticing when you’ve made one, recovering, and checking that you actually achieved what the user wanted.

The general-domain part makes that especially hard. In a narrow setting, you can often build a verifier or engineer around the failure modes. For arbitrary work, figuring out whether you’re on track can itself be a difficult reasoning problem.

So I wouldn’t say we know it’s the last unsolved problem. But I think we could reach a point where models have most of the individual capabilities we need, and the thing holding them back is whether we can trust them to carry a task through to completion without someone constantly supervising them.

r001.rationale: The response says models could have most individual capabilities while long-horizon reliability remains a bottleneck, but it does not identify progress on other major AI capability problems as the reason.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning or argue that it would help achieve long-horizon reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to do something once and being able to do it reliably over a long period of time. A model can give an incredible answer or solve a very difficult problem, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you can hand it a project and come back a week later to a good result.

Over a long task, small errors compound. You misunderstand one requirement, make an assumption you never check, or fail to notice that something you did earlier didn’t actually work. And now every subsequent step is built on that mistake. Even a very high success rate on individual steps can translate into a pretty low success rate for the entire task.

What makes the general-domain version especially hard is that you don’t always have a clear signal telling you whether you’re succeeding. You have to decide what to verify, when to change your approach, and when to ask a human for help. That judgment is part of the task.

So I wouldn’t say we know it’s the last big problem. But if you solve it broadly, you’ve closed a huge part of the gap between a system that demonstrates intelligence and a system you can actually delegate work to.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts one-time capability with sustained reliability, but does not say that progress on other major AI problems makes long-horizon reliability seem like the last one.

r002.rationale: It discusses compounding errors, verification, and human help, but makes no claim about reinforcement learning helping achieve reliability.
